newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says Solidarity tax to go in 1999.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says Solidarity tax to go in 1999.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Tuesday the Solidarity Surcharge on income tax, which is to be reduced next year, would disappear entirely when Bonn implemented a comprehensive tax reform in 1999.
Waigel told a parliamentary budget debate: "When we introduce the tax reform the Solidarity Surcharge will belong to the past."

The 7.5 percent surcharge on income tax was reintroduced in 1995 to help pay for the enormous costs related to German unification. Bonn plans to cut it to 6.5 percent next year and 5.5 percent in 1998.
Waigel said the aim of the 1999 tax reform was a simplification of a system which had become far too complex as well as a net reduction in taxes.
"But the principle of a socially just taxation system will remain," he said.
Waigel has been under considerable pressure recently to implement the tax reform in 1998, a year earlier than planned but has so far resisted.
He repeated on Tuesday that a commission studying reform proposals would come forward with concrete recommendations by the end of this year.
The top income tax rate would fall to under 40 percent from the current 53 percent and the lowest rate would be cut to around 20 percent from the current 26 percent, he said.
He called on the opposition Social Democrats not to block the planned scrapping of the capital trading tax and wealth tax on operating assets next year.
